claims.text: The starting material is cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has acceptable high-temperature yield strength.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has inadequate oxygen or oxidation resistance.
The proposed single intervention is a pack-aluminizing diffusion treatment.
Pack aluminizing will produce a thin Al-rich or alumina-rich surface layer on equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The pack-aluminized surface layer will be adherent.
The aluminide layer will react with oxygen at elevated temperature to form a continuous protective Al2O3 scale.
The Al2O3 scale will limit oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy.
Pack-aluminized material will have lower oxygen uptake than untreated material.
Pack-aluminized material will retain a more intact and adherent alumina scale than untreated material.
Pack aluminizing will preserve room- and high-temperature ductility and yield strength at levels similar to untreated material.
The intervention is applicable to air exposures from 800 to 1000 °C for up to 5 hours.
The relevant loading boundary is a strain-rate range of 10^-4 to 10^-2 s^-1.
Avoiding significant alteration of the alloy's bulk composition is necessary to preserve its mechanical properties.
Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr undergoes pesting or degradation under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
The thickness, integrity, and long-term adherence of the alumina scale under cyclic or extended exposure are undetermined.

contradictions.description: The treatment is initially said to form an alumina-rich layer, whereas the mechanism says it first forms an aluminide layer that subsequently oxidizes into alumina; the identity and timing of the mediator are inconsistent.
The conditions and boundary describe oxidation exposure as occurring under specified strain rates, but the experiment describes an unloaded oxidation exposure followed by separate tensile tests.
